messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Editor
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 56

He is a 26-year-old South Asian man who works as an editor and comes across in session as careful, articulate, and constantly alert to what might be left unsaid. He is married, and he speaks about his wife with warmth, though also with a kind of distance that seems to come from exhaustion rather than lack of feeling. Before the traumatic event, he describes himself as someone who liked order, deadlines, and the quiet satisfaction of shaping messy material into something coherent. Editing gave him a sense of control. He could sit with a draft for hours, notice every misplaced word, and make things right.

That sense of control changes after an encounter with police that he still describes in fragments, as if the memory arrives in broken pieces before he can fully arrange it. He had been out in public when he is stopped, questioned, and treated as if he is already guilty. What begins as confusion quickly turns into fear. He remembers the tone of voices, the physical intimidation, the humiliation of being spoken to like someone without rights. He does not talk about the event as a single dramatic moment so much as an escalating series of violations: being told to stand still, being searched, being dismissed when he tries to explain himself. The experience leaves him shaken in a way he does not understand at first, because he had assumed that compliance would protect him. Instead, compliance seems to make him feel smaller.

In the days afterward, he tells himself it is over and that he should get back to work. He returns to his editing tasks, but he finds that he cannot concentrate the way he used to. A sentence on the page can suddenly blur, and he realizes he has read the same line several times without taking it in. He becomes more irritable with minor mistakes and then feels ashamed of his sharpness. He starts checking doors more than once and listening closely whenever he hears footsteps outside. The sound of a siren makes his stomach drop before he can reason with himself. He notices that his body reacts before his mind catches up: tight chest, dry mouth, muscles clenched as if bracing for impact.

At home, his wife sees that he is not sleeping well. He falls asleep late and wakes often, sometimes because of dreams he does not want to describe in detail. He only says that he wakes with his heart racing and an immediate sense that something bad is about to happen. After these nights, he moves through the day as if he has not fully returned to himself. He becomes quieter at dinner, less present in conversation, and he starts sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants. He avoids routes that bring him near police presence, and if he sees an officer nearby he feels a sudden surge of heat in his face and an urge to leave quickly. He does not like how aware he has become of uniforms, radios, and authoritative voices, because each of them pulls him back into the same helpless feeling.

He finds that he is not only avoiding places but also memories. When friends ask what happened, he gives short answers or changes the subject. He does not want to see himself as someone who was frightened in public, and part of him worries that if he talks too much, the memory will become more real. Yet the opposite seems to happen: the less he says, the more it presses in on him. He has moments when he suddenly feels back there, hearing the same tone of voice, and he freezes for a second before he can orient himself. He says he feels “on edge all the time,” as if his body never fully gets the message that he is safe.

Over time, this changed state begins to affect how he sees himself. He used to take pride in being composed, efficient, and dependable. Now he worries that he is failing at ordinary life because he cannot relax, cannot focus, and cannot simply “move on” the way others seem to expect. He feels embarrassed by how quickly he startles and frustrated by the way his mind keeps returning to the event. His marriage becomes a quiet source of strain, not because he stops caring, but because he often feels emotionally numb or preoccupied when he wants to be present. He misses the version of himself who could make sense of things neatly. In therapy, he speaks as if he is still trying to edit the experience into something survivable, though the story refuses to come into clean order.
